lesson.title: Finding the Typical Value: What Center Really Means
lesson.summary: The center of a distribution is the value around which the data seems to cluster, and choosing how to measure it, whether by mean, median, or mode, depends heavily on the distribution's shape.
lesson.body:
Whenever you summarize a distribution, one of the first questions worth answering is: where is the center? The center of a distribution is loosely defined as the value or small range of values around which the data seems to cluster, the answer to the question "if I had to pick one number to represent this whole data set, what would it be?" Center is one of the handful of features, alongside shape, spread, and outliers, that together give a complete description of any distribution, and it is impossible to fully describe a data set without addressing it.

The tricky part is that "center" is not a single, unambiguous number, it can be measured in more than one way, and different methods can give noticeably different answers depending on the shape of the distribution. The three standard measures, covered individually later in this unit, are the mean, which is the arithmetic average of all values, the median, which is the middle value when the data is sorted, and the mode, which is the most frequently occurring value. Each measure answers the question "where is the center" from a slightly different angle, and none of them is universally the correct one, the right choice depends on context and, critically, on shape.

Consider six people's ages: 22, 23, 24, 24, 25, and 60. Sorted, the median, the average of the third and fourth values, is (24 + 24) divided by 2, which is 24. The mean is the sum divided by six: 22 + 23 + 24 + 24 + 25 + 60 = 178, and 178 divided by 6 is about 29.67. Notice that these two measures of center disagree by more than five years. The median, 24, matches what five of the six people's ages actually look like, while the mean, 29.67, is pulled upward by the single 60-year-old and does not resemble any single person's actual age particularly well.

This disagreement is not a flaw in either measure, it is a direct consequence of the shape of the distribution, specifically the right skew created by the age-60 outlier, connecting this idea back to both the skewed-right and outlier concepts covered earlier in this unit. When a distribution is roughly symmetric, the mean and median tend to agree closely and either one describes the center well. When a distribution is skewed or contains outliers, the mean and median can diverge substantially, and choosing which one to report, or reporting both, becomes an important judgment call rather than a formality.

Center should never be reported without also describing shape, since the two are so tightly linked: a stated center means little on its own unless the reader also knows whether it came from a symmetric, left-skewed, or right-skewed distribution, and whether it was pulled by an outlier along the way.

Understanding center as a concept, before diving into the mechanics of computing each specific measure, sets up the rest of this unit: the sections ahead on mean, median, and mode are really three different techniques for answering the same underlying question, each with its own strengths, weaknesses, and best-use situations depending on what the distribution's shape looks like.
